kf1.tip: Draw from memory a flow chart of blood from the vena cava to the aorta, then mark each stage as oxygenated or deoxygenated.
kf1.note: Your chart should run in this order: vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta. Everything before the lungs is deoxygenated. Everything after is oxygenated, because gas exchange in the lungs swaps carbon dioxide for oxygen. Check the pulmonary artery. If you marked it oxygenated, you fell into the usual trap. It is an artery, but it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

kf2.tip: Predict whether Q at 200 bpm and a stroke volume of 110 ml beats 20,000 ml/min, then check it using the formula, the substitution and the unit.
kf2.note: Yes, it beats 20,000 ml/min. Start with the formula: Q = stroke volume × heart rate. Then substitute: Q = 110 ml × 200 bpm = 22,000 ml/min, which is 22 L/min. If you left off the unit or skipped the formula line, your answer is incomplete. This fits the lesson's figure of 20 to 25 litres per minute for a trained athlete at intense exercise.

cs1.tip: Pick a sport you play and name the body areas where vasoconstriction and vasodilation would act during a match, then explain the vascular shunt.
cs1.note: A good answer names the muscles your sport works hardest as the place where vasodilation widens vessels and sends more blood. It names an inactive area, such as the digestive system, where vasoconstriction narrows vessels and reduces blood flow. It then says the vascular shunt is this redistribution of blood. A weak answer forgets the reason: working muscles need much more oxygen and glucose. It also mixes up which mechanism widens and which narrows.
